SECTION GUIDE - MK

ASVAB Mathematics Knowledge

What it tests, how it is scored, full lessons, and 10 practice questions with answers

What MK Tests

Mathematics Knowledge (MK) tests high-school math directly: algebra, equations and inequalities, exponents and roots, factoring, geometry (area, perimeter, volume, angles, triangles, circles), and basic probability. No calculator is allowed.

Scored questions (CAT-ASVAB)15
Time limit31 minutes (about 124 seconds per question)
Part of the AFQT?Yes

MK is one of the four AFQT sections. It also feeds the Army CL, EL, FA, GM, and ST line scores. See ASVAB scores explained for how section scores become your AFQT and line scores.

How to Score Higher

  • Memorize the core formulas. The real test gives you none of them.
  • Plug the answer choices back in when an equation looks messy. One of the four has to work.
  • Check for extraneous answers. A value that makes a denominator zero is never a solution.
  • When a figure is scaled by k, areas scale by k squared and volumes by k cubed.

Mathematics Knowledge Lessons

Algebra and geometry concepts. Each lesson below is also in the interactive study guide, where you can take a quiz to check yourself.

  1. Solving Equations
  2. Exponents & Radicals
  3. FOIL & Factoring
  4. Pythagorean Theorem
  5. Area & Perimeter
  6. Inequalities

Lesson 1 Solving Equations

Equations are like a balance scale. Whatever you do to one side, you MUST do to the other. Once you get this, algebra becomes straightforward.

The Balance Rule

An equation is balanced. To keep it balanced, any operation you do to the left side, you must do to the right side too. Add 5 to the left? Add 5 to the right.

Isolating the Variable

Your goal is to get x (or whatever variable) alone on one side. Do this by 'undoing' operations in reverse order: first add/subtract, then multiply/divide.

Variables on Both Sides

If x appears on both sides, first move all x terms to one side by adding or subtracting. Then solve as usual.

Worked example

Solve: 3x + 7 = 22

  1. Subtract 7 from both sides: 3x = 15
  2. Divide both sides by 3: x = 5
  3. Check: 3(5) + 7 = 15 + 7 = 22 ✓

Tip: Always check your answer by plugging it back in!

Worked example

Solve: 5x - 8 = 2x + 7

  1. Subtract 2x from both sides: 3x - 8 = 7
  2. Add 8 to both sides: 3x = 15
  3. Divide by 3: x = 5

Tip: Move all x terms to the side with the larger coefficient.

Key takeaway: To solve any equation: (1) Move variables to one side, (2) Move numbers to the other side, (3) Divide by the coefficient. Always check your answer.

Lesson 2 Exponents & Radicals

Exponents are just shorthand for repeated multiplication. x³ means x × x × x. Once you learn the rules, these problems become quick wins.

Multiplying Same Base = ADD Exponents

x³ × x⁴ = x⁷. Why? Because (x·x·x) × (x·x·x·x) = x⁷. When multiplying same bases, add the exponents.

Dividing Same Base = SUBTRACT Exponents

x⁸ ÷ x³ = x⁵. You're canceling out 3 of the x's from the 8, leaving 5.

Power of a Power = MULTIPLY Exponents

(x³)² = x⁶. You're squaring x³, which means x³ × x³ = x⁶.

Special Cases

x⁰ = 1 (anything to the zero power is 1). x⁻ⁿ = 1/xⁿ (negative exponent means reciprocal).

Worked example

Simplify: x⁵ × x³

  1. Same base (x), so ADD exponents
  2. x⁵⁺³ = x⁸

Tip: ADD for multiplication, SUBTRACT for division.

Worked example

Simplify: (x⁴)³

  1. Power of a power: MULTIPLY exponents
  2. x⁴ˣ³ = x¹²

Tip: MULTIPLY when you have an exponent raised to another exponent.

Key takeaway: Three rules: Multiply same base → ADD exponents. Divide same base → SUBTRACT. Power of power → MULTIPLY. x⁰ = 1.

Lesson 3 FOIL & Factoring

FOIL is a method for multiplying two binomials. Factoring is the reverse: breaking an expression back into two binomials. Master both!

FOIL: First, Outer, Inner, Last

To multiply (a + b)(c + d): First (a×c), Outer (a×d), Inner (b×c), Last (b×d). Then combine like terms.

Factoring x² + bx + c

Find two numbers that MULTIPLY to c and ADD to b. Those become your factors: (x + ?)(x + ?).

Difference of Squares

a² - b² = (a + b)(a - b). This is a special pattern. Example: x² - 9 = (x + 3)(x - 3).

Worked example

Expand: (x + 3)(x + 5)

  1. First: x × x = x²
  2. Outer: x × 5 = 5x
  3. Inner: 3 × x = 3x
  4. Last: 3 × 5 = 15
  5. Combine: x² + 5x + 3x + 15 = x² + 8x + 15

Tip: Watch your signs! A negative in either binomial changes signs.

Worked example

Factor: x² + 7x + 12

  1. Need two numbers that multiply to 12 and add to 7
  2. 3 × 4 = 12 ✓ and 3 + 4 = 7 ✓
  3. Answer: (x + 3)(x + 4)

Tip: Always check by FOILing your answer back out!

Key takeaway: FOIL: First-Outer-Inner-Last, then combine like terms. Factoring: find two numbers that multiply to the constant and add to the middle coefficient.

Lesson 4 Pythagorean Theorem

The Pythagorean Theorem is THE most tested geometry concept. It only works for right triangles (with a 90° angle).

The Formula

a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse (longest side, across from the right angle). a and b are the legs.

Pythagorean Triples

Memorize these! 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25. Multiples work too: 6-8-10 (double 3-4-5).

Finding a Leg

If you need to find a leg, rearrange: a² = c² - b². Then take the square root.

Worked example

A right triangle has legs 3 and 4. Find the hypotenuse.

  1. a² + b² = c²
  2. 3² + 4² = c²
  3. 9 + 16 = 25 = c²
  4. c = 5

Tip: 3-4-5 is the most common Pythagorean triple!

Worked example

A right triangle has hypotenuse 13 and one leg 5. Find the other leg.

  1. a² + 5² = 13²
  2. a² + 25 = 169
  3. a² = 144
  4. a = 12

Tip: Recognize 5-12-13 triple? It saves calculation time!

Key takeaway: a² + b² = c² (c is hypotenuse). Memorize triples: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17. The hypotenuse is ALWAYS the longest side.

Lesson 5 Area & Perimeter

These formulas come up constantly. Memorize them, there's no formula sheet on the ASVAB!

Rectangle

Area = length × width. Perimeter = 2(length) + 2(width) or 2(l + w).

Triangle

Area = ½ × base × height. The height must be perpendicular to the base!

Circle

Area = πr². Circumference = 2πr = πd. Always use RADIUS, not diameter!

Worked example

Find the area of a rectangle with length 8 and width 5.

  1. Area = length × width
  2. Area = 8 × 5 = 40 square units

Tip: Area is always in square units (sq ft, sq m, etc.)

Worked example

Find the area of a circle with diameter 10.

  1. Diameter = 10, so radius = 5
  2. Area = πr² = π(5)² = 25π

Tip: ALWAYS use radius, not diameter. If given diameter, divide by 2 first!

Key takeaway: Rectangle: A = lw, P = 2l + 2w. Triangle: A = ½bh. Circle: A = πr², C = 2πr. Use RADIUS for circles!

Lesson 6 Inequalities

Inequalities are solved just like equations, with ONE critical rule: flip the sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative!

Solving Inequalities

Solve exactly like equations: add, subtract, multiply, divide. But there's one exception...

THE FLIP RULE

When you multiply or divide both sides by a NEGATIVE number, FLIP the inequality sign. > becomes <. ≥ becomes ≤.

Reading Inequality Signs

< means less than. > means greater than. ≤ means less than or equal. ≥ means greater than or equal.

Worked example

Solve: 3x + 5 > 14

  1. Subtract 5: 3x > 9
  2. Divide by 3: x > 3
  3. No flip needed (divided by positive)

Tip: No negative division = no flip needed.

Worked example

Solve: -2x + 4 ≤ 10

  1. Subtract 4: -2x ≤ 6
  2. Divide by -2 AND FLIP: x ≥ -3
  3. Sign changed from ≤ to ≥ because we divided by negative!

Tip: Divided by negative = MUST flip the sign!

Key takeaway: Solve like equations. FLIP the inequality sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number.

MK Practice Questions

Try each question before opening the answer. On the real CAT-ASVAB the questions adapt to you, so a timed, adaptive practice test is the best way to check your level.

Question 1

What is the area of a triangle with base 8 and height 6?

  1. 48 square units
  2. 24 square units
  3. 14 square units
  4. 28 square units
Show answer

Answer: B. 24 square units

Area of a triangle = 1/2 × base × height. Here that is 1/2 × 8 × 6 = 1/2 × 48 = 24 square units. Remember the one-half factor that separates a triangle from a rectangle.

Question 2

In a right triangle, if one leg is 3 and the other is 4, what is the hypotenuse?

  1. 5
  2. 6
  3. 7
  4. 12
Show answer

Answer: A. 5

Use the Pythagorean theorem: leg² + leg² = hypotenuse². Here 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25, and the square root of 25 is 5. This is the classic 3-4-5 triangle.

Question 3

Solve for x: 3(x + 1) = 5(x - 2) + 7

  1. -2
  2. 2
  3. 1/2
  4. 3
Show answer

Answer: D. 3

Expand both sides: 3x + 3 = 5x − 10 + 7 = 5x − 3. Subtract 3x and add 3: 6 = 2x, so x = 3. Distribute first, then collect variables on one side.

Question 4

Simplify: 3x + 2 - (4x - 6)

  1. -x + 8
  2. -x - 8
  3. x + 8
  4. x - 8
Show answer

Answer: A. -x + 8

Distribute the negative: 3x + 2 − 4x + 6 = −x + 8. Subtracting a group flips every sign inside it.

Question 5

A rectangle is cut in half to create two squares, each with area 25. What is the perimeter of the original rectangle?

  1. 20
  2. 25
  3. 30
  4. 50
Show answer

Answer: C. 30

Each square has area 25, so each side is 5. Two squares side by side form a rectangle 10 by 5, giving perimeter 2(10 + 5) = 30.

Question 6

Simplify: (3⁴) ÷ (3²)

  1. 3²
  2. 3⁶
  3. 3⁸
  4. 9
Show answer

Answer: A. 3²

Dividing like bases subtracts exponents: 3⁴ ÷ 3² = 3^(4−2) = 3². Keep the same base and subtract.

Question 7

What is the area of a circle with radius 6? (Use π = 3.14)

  1. 18.84 sq units
  2. 37.68 sq units
  3. 113.04 sq units
  4. 56.52 sq units
Show answer

Answer: C. 113.04 sq units

Area of a circle = πr² = 3.14 × 6² = 3.14 × 36 = 113.04 square units. Square the radius, then multiply by π.

Question 8

Solve: x + 5 > 12. What values satisfy this inequality?

  1. x > 7
  2. x < 7
  3. x > 17
  4. x < 17
Show answer

Answer: A. x > 7

Subtract 5 from both sides of x + 5 greater than 12 to get x greater than 7. Solve an inequality like an equation, keeping the direction.

Question 9

Factor: x² - 25

  1. (x + 5)(x + 5)
  2. (x - 5)(x - 5)
  3. (x + 5)(x - 5)
  4. (x + 25)(x - 1)
Show answer

Answer: C. (x + 5)(x - 5)

This is a difference of squares, a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b). With a = x and b = 5, x² − 25 = (x + 5)(x − 5).

Question 10

If the area of a circle is 100π square units, what is the radius?

  1. 5 units
  2. 10 units
  3. 25 units
  4. 50 units
Show answer

Answer: B. 10 units

Area of a circle = πr². Set πr² = 100π, so r² = 100 and r = √100 = 10 units. Divide out π, then take the square root.
